title: Teleprinters were tested by typing RYRYRY, because R and Y are exact opposites

cover.alt: Close-up of an old black teleprinter with a white paper roll, on which short lines of test text have been printed.

body: Teleprinters sent each character as five on-or-off pulses, in the 5-bit code known as ITA2 or Baudot. In that code **R is 01010 and Y is 10101**: every pulse of one is the reverse of the other. Sending R and Y in turn therefore flips all five pulses with every character, which made RYRYRY a hard workout for an electromechanical teleprinter and a standard test for its line. Technicians used RY test tapes to align their equipment, and RYRYRY was often sent at the start of transmissions.

slides.alt: A teleprinter's paper roll creeps up as its mechanism prints line after line of test text, with two ribbon spools in front.
slides.caption: A Lorenz Lo15 teleprinter in a former telecoms centre in Elmshorn, Germany, fed by a test generator, prints line after line ending in 'ryry'.
slides.music: “Mighty Like Us” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.question: With 5 on-or-off pulses per character, how many different codes can a teleprinter send?
slides.explanation: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. Not enough for letters and numbers, so keyboards had LTRS and FIGS keys to switch between two sets.

slides.prompt: If the signal's polarity was reversed, the RY test printed two other letters. Which?
slides.detail: Seeing SG where RY should be told technicians the polarity was the wrong way round.

slides.heading: Built to save wear
slides.text: In 1901 Donald Murray reworked [Baudot's code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baudot_code) so that the commonest letters had the fewest holes on punched tape: E and T have just one. In the 7-bit ASCII code that came later, the matching test pair is U and *.
